note: The row-parity oracle. Each rule is translated to a WHERE clause and run
against the fixture, and evaluated by SEL over the same rows loaded as a
context. The two id lists must match.
This is the only oracle that exercises the `relation` binding, because a
correlated subquery has nothing to correlate to without a query around it.
The closed corpus in expressions.selo covers everything that does not need
a table; this covers what does.
`expect` is not the answer being asserted -- the answer is whatever SEL
says. It is a guard that the fixture still makes the rule discriminate:
the driver fails if a rule selects every order or none, because a rule that
does agrees for no reason.

`correlate.raw` is raw SQL by design -- it is the one place a host says something the map cannot know -- and raw SQL does not travel between dialects. So it is written per dialect here, and the driver picks. Backticks are MySQL-family and SQLite; PostgreSQL wants double quotes.
A rule may also state that a dialect REFUSES it (`refuse`, per dialect),
which rows over a text column SEL itself refuses (`raises`), and -- only for
docs/internals/sql-kinds.md section 6's exclusion 4 -- an answer the database is
allowed to give that SEL does not (`database`, with `excluded` saying why).
Refused rows are absent from what SEL selects, so the ordinary comparison is
the warrant: SQL must not report a match for a row SEL would not answer for.
`ansi-probe` appears beside the four servers in every per-dialect `raw`. It is
not a server: php/bin/sqlo registers it to reach the ansi entries no target
resolves, and it needs a correlation here only so the relation skeletons are
counted as covered under it. The spelling is PostgreSQL's, which is the
standard's -- double-quoted identifiers -- and there is no fixture for it, so
run_rows skips it and only coverage reads this.
select: SELECT id FROM o WHERE {} ORDER BY id

context.query: SELECT id, credit_limit, code, code AS code_u, code AS code_x FROM o ORDER BY id

ITEMS.query: SELECT order_id, qty, price, sku, value, value AS value_u FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

SKUS.query: SELECT order_id, sku FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

NOTES.query: SELECT order_id, note FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

rules.name: all lines have quantity
any big line
has no lines
over credit limit
empty lines counted
all skus well formed
filtered lines all cheap
sku in the line set
rules.note: SKUS projects one column, so SEL reads it as a list of scalars and IN means the same thing on both sides. IN over the multi-field ITEMS is refused; see the refusal case in sql/cases/09-refusals.sqlt.

rules.name: sku matches, exact case
sku matches, wrong case
rules.degenerate: Empty is the point. The fixture's columns are utf8mb4_general_ci, so a server comparing them under the column collation answers [1] and SEL answers []. This rule is the collation carried into a correlated subquery, which nothing else here checks.

rules.name: a NULL among the rows must not swallow a NOT
a NULL inside an ALL body is not a failed row
a NULL matched positively still answers
a text column compared as a number
rules.why: The report this came from, reduced: a VARCHAR column of EAV values compared numerically. MariaDB reads '25/298' as 25 and 'x' and '' as 0, so before the guard this selected orders 1, 2, 3 and 4 -- three of them rows SEL refuses. sqlite cannot ask whether a value is a number -- no REGEXP, and CAST answers 0 for 'abc' rather than saying so -- so it has no numericGuard and the rule is refused rather than emitted unguarded. docs/internals/sql-kinds.md section 5.

rules.name: an undeclared column compared as a number
rules.why: The same column with no declared type, which is what an application gets when it does not say. UNKNOWN takes the guard for the same reason TEXT does, and this is the only place that path is measured against a server.

rules.name: arithmetic over a text column
rules.why: Comparison is not the only numeric context. `* 1` is also the workaround docs/internals/sql-kinds.md section 4.1a offers for the function-argument family, so this is the rule that says the workaround actually works on a server.

rules.name: the guard inside a correlated subquery
rules.why: ALL needs no exclusion: it refuses on any bad element whatever the order, and NOT EXISTS (... IS NOT TRUE) turns the guard's NULL into FALSE. Orders 1 and 2 hold a non-numeric value and SEL refuses both; order 4 answers FALSE on a numeric 0 without reaching anything bad.

rules.name: ANY over a relation with one bad element
rules.why: docs/internals/sql-kinds.md section 6, exclusion 4, made runnable. SEL's ANY short-circuits, so it reaches AB-1000's 'x' first and refuses order 1; SQL's EXISTS has no order and answers TRUE on CD-2000's 9. SEL has no single answer to be faithful to -- the other ordering answers TRUE -- so the warrant holds only in its weakened form. The guard changes nothing here either way, and order 2, whose only element is bad, is excluded by both sides.
rules.excluded: SQL-KINDS.md section 6 exclusion 4: ANY short-circuits and a relation has no order

rules.name: an undeclared column used as a boolean
rules.why: The other half of the warrant, and the half with no guard: no dialect can ask whether a value is a boolean, because in the MySQL family a boolean IS a TINYINT. Every dialect refuses, so no server is reached -- which is the point.

rules.name: the comparison that matched every row
rules.why: The report as written: `T == 0` over a text column. MariaDB casts both 'x' and '' to 0, so this selected orders 3 and 4 -- rows SEL refuses -- and on a table of non-numeric values it selects all of them. It selects nothing now, and nothing is what SEL selects: order 1 is '25' and order 5 is '30', both FALSE, and the other three SEL refuses outright. Declared degenerate because an empty answer is the whole point here, not a fixture that stopped discriminating.
rules.degenerate: selects nothing, and that is the assertion

rules.name: is-blank over a text column
rules.why: Tests IS_BLANK against a column containing both non-empty and empty strings. Order 4 is '' and must match; orders 1, 2, 3, 5 are non-empty and must not.

rules.name: is-present over a text column
rules.why: Inverse of IS_BLANK. Orders 1, 2, 3, 5 are non-empty and must match; order 4 is '' and must not.

rules.name: vacuous coalescing over a text column
rules.why: Tests ??? replacing an empty string with a fallback. Order 4 is '' so ??? yields 'empty', matching the comparison; the other orders keep their non-empty code.

rules.name: min over a numeric column and a numeric literal
rules.why: SQLite's multi-argument min() ranks every number below every text value, so a literal emitted as '60' loses to nothing: min(100.0, '60') is 100.0, and MIN(CREDIT_LIMIT, 60) > 70 selected orders SEL says are at most 60. The OR arm keeps the rule discriminating.

rules.name: max over a numeric column and a numeric literal
rules.why: The mirror: max(500.0, '60') is '60' in SQLite, so MAX(CREDIT_LIMIT, 60) > 400 selected nothing where SEL selects order 3.

rules.name: exact text column against a numeric item
rules.why: An `exact` column skips the byte cast on the column, so a NUMBER item beside it must be cast to text too: bare `code = 25` makes MariaDB/MySQL compare numerically ('25/298' = 25 is TRUE by numeric prefix) and SQLite compare under the column's affinity, matches SEL refuses (SEL's IN is EQL: structural, '25' IN ("a", 25) is TRUE only for the row holding exactly '25').

rules.name: conditional over an undeclared column, guarded as a whole
rules.why: `??` replaces only NULL, so 'x' stays 'x' and SEL raises E_NOT_NUM. A guard placed on the LEAF, COALESCE(guard(code), '1'), turns 'x' into NULL and then into '1', and `+ 1 > 0` selects order 3 where SEL selects nothing for it. The guard has to wrap the whole conditional (docs/internals/sql-kinds.md 5a). Orders 1 and 5 hold '25' and '30'; 2 ('25/298'), 3 ('x') and 4 ('') are refused rows.

rules.name: sum over an undeclared field, all or nothing
rules.why: SUM skips NULL and the layer wraps COALESCE(SUM(..), 0) around it, so a per-element guard turns a refused element into a missing one: order 1 (values 'x', '9') would be 9 and order 2 ('n/a') would be 0, both >= 0, where SEL raises E_NOT_NUM for both. The guarded form makes the whole SUM NULL when any element fails the numeric test (docs/internals/sql-kinds.md 5a). Order 3 has no lines (0), order 4 sums to 4 and order 5 to 3.

rules.name: scope: an inlined helper is not captured by a later binder
rules.why: X = CREDIT_LIMIT + 1 is written where CREDIT_LIMIT is the column, so inside the body CREDIT_LIMIT < X compares the element with the column plus one and only order 3 (500) holds for the element 200. Substituting by name lets the binder capture X's free name: every element is below itself plus one and every order is selected.
rules.sel: X = CREDIT_LIMIT + 1; ALL((5, 60, 200), CREDIT_LIMIT, CREDIT_LIMIT < X)

rules.name: scope: a helper read inside a same-named binder body keeps the column
rules.why: X = CREDIT_LIMIT is the column; the binder that reuses the name shadows it only in its own body, where X still means the column. Captured, X > 60 is constantly FALSE.

rules.name: scope: a FILTER's binder is not in scope in the consuming aggregate
rules.why: The FILTER binder is named like the column, so leaking it into the body would compare each element with itself; the body's CREDIT_LIMIT is the column and only order 3 exceeds 400.
rules.sel: ALL(FILTER((40,60,400), CREDIT_LIMIT, CREDIT_LIMIT > 50), Y, Y < CREDIT_LIMIT)

rules.name: scope: an indexed-assignment list is copied, not aliased
rules.why: X = R copies (spec 3.4); R[2] = 0 afterwards is not in X, so COUNT(X) is 1. Aliased it is 2 and the rule selects nothing.
rules.sel: R[1] = CREDIT_LIMIT; X = R; R[2] = 0; COUNT(X) == 1 AND CREDIT_LIMIT > 20

rules.name: scope: a binder reusing the row binder's name in an inner list
rules.why: Over a relation: the inner list's I["QTY"] is the OUTER row; the inner body's I is the inner element. It equals ANY(ITEMS, I, I["QTY"] > 1).

rules.name: scope: an inner list mixing the outer row and an outer column
rules.why: The list reads the outer row's QTY and the order's CREDIT_LIMIT, the body a fresh binder; orders 2 and 5 have a line of quantity 5 or more.
rules.sel: ANY(ITEMS, I, ALL((I["QTY"], CREDIT_LIMIT), Q, Q >= 5))

rules.name: scope: _K in an inner list is the OUTER element's key
rules.why: The outer iterations are "1" and "2"; the inner list's _K is that key, not the inner binder's, so the second iteration holds "2" and the body is TRUE. Using the inner key "1" in both halves makes it constantly FALSE; the AND keeps the rule from selecting every order. Text comparison only, so every dialect can translate it.
rules.sel: ANY((0,0), ANY((_K, "zz"), c, c $== "2")) AND CREDIT_LIMIT > 20
